sessions.title: Natural energy
script: Good morning. Your body's a bit sluggish today, and that's normal. Let's wake it up together, no coffee needed.
You can stand up, or stay sitting on the edge of the bed with your feet flat on the floor. Either works.
Let your arms hang loose. Lengthen a little, as if a thread were drawing the top of your head upward.
We'll start with the breath. Three brisk breaths in through the nose, and three firm breaths out through the mouth, like a big audible sigh.
Here we go. Breathe in sharply through your nose.
And blow it all out, in one go, through your mouth.
Again. Breathe in, quick and clean, opening the chest.
And let go. Let the air rush out like a balloon you've just released.
One last time. In… and out.
[pause 3s]
Now come back to your usual breathing. If you feel a little light-headed, just breathe easily; it passes in a few seconds.
These three brisker breaths send your body a simple signal: the night is over, time to get going. Three is plenty.
Notice the difference already. Maybe a bit more warmth in your face, a bit more air in your ribcage.
Now, a stretch. Breathing in, raise both arms toward the sky, fingers spread.
Press your palms gently upward. Feel your ribs widening, your belly lengthening, the space opening up under your arms.
If you're standing, you can even rise up a little onto your toes.
[pause 3s]
Breathing out, let your arms float down slowly, like wings folding in.
One more time: arms rise as you breathe in… and come down as you breathe out.
Now for some tapping. With your right hand, palm soft, tap along your left arm. Work from the shoulder down to the wrist, then back up the inside of the arm.
No need to tap hard. Just enough to feel the skin waking up.
Tapping like this wakes up the circulation under your skin, a bit like shaking out a duvet to fluff it up.
Switch sides: your left hand taps along your right arm, from shoulder to hand, and back again.
Now both hands to the top of your chest, below the collarbones. Light little taps with your fingertips, like soft rain.
Then your shoulders, and the back of your neck, where the night often leaves some stiffness.
Move down to your thighs, tapping the tops and outsides down to your knees. If you're standing, only bend as far as is comfortable.
Stop. Let your hands rest. Feel the tingling, the warmth, as if your skin had just been switched on.
Now roll your shoulders backward. Big, slow circles: up toward your ears, back, and down.
Three times… then three times the other way.
[pause 3s]
Next, your neck. Let your chin drop gently toward your chest.
Roll your head toward your right shoulder, through the center, then to the left. A half circle, always through the front, never backward.
Only go where it feels good. Never into pain.
If your neck or shoulders are sensitive, simply make the movement smaller. A little goes a long way.
Come back to center. Breathe normally, without changing a thing.
Take a few seconds to feel what's moving through you. Your hands, your arms, your face. Maybe a faint buzzing, a sense of being a little more here.
This isn't energy borrowed from somewhere else. It's your own, simply woken up.
[pause 3s]
Before you go, choose one concrete first step for your day. Open the curtains, drink a big glass of water, put on some music, step outside for some fresh air.
Just one thing, simple, that you can do right now.
Got it? Then off you go. Your day starts now.

sessions.title: The first coffee
script: You've got a cup in your hands, or you're about to pick one up. Coffee, tea, hot water, a plain glass of water: anything works.
For the next five minutes, this drink is your meditation. Nothing else to do but drink it, properly.
If your phone is in front of you, turn it face down, or put it a little further away. Your messages can wait for the length of one cup.
Sit down if you can. Feet on the floor, back supported.
[pause 3s]
Hold the cup in both hands. Wrap them all the way around it, fingers almost touching.
Let a first breath out, a long one, like a sigh that says: right, here I am.
And another, if you like. Shoulders drop a little, hands still resting around the cup.
Feel the warmth in your palms. Where is it strongest? Maybe in the hollow of your hand, maybe at your fingertips.
Notice how it spreads. It moves up into your wrists, sometimes as far as your forearms.
Notice the weight of the cup, too. Its texture. Smooth, a little rough, a tiny flaw in the glaze, the curve of the handle.
These are things you touch every single day, without ever really feeling them.
[pause 3s]
Now bring the cup up toward your face, without drinking just yet.
Feel the steam on your skin, under your nose, on your lips.
Breathe in slowly through your nose. Let the aroma in.
No need to fill your lungs. A slow, light breath is enough to let the scent arrive.

What can you smell? Something roasted, toasty, maybe a little chocolatey. Or something floral, grassy, if it's tea. And if it's water, almost nothing… and that almost-nothing is something you can notice too.
Breathe in again, more softly. Sometimes a second note appears, quieter than the first.
Notice what's happening in your mouth as well. The saliva gathering, your body getting ready. It already knows what's coming.
Now, the first sip. A small one. Hold it in your mouth for a moment before you swallow.
Feel the temperature first. Hot, scalding, lukewarm.
Then the taste. Where does it land first? The tip of your tongue, the sides, the back?
Bitter, sweet, sharp, smooth… No need to find the right word. Just taste.
And when you're ready, swallow. Follow the path it takes. Down your throat, then that warmth sliding down behind your breastbone, all the way to your stomach.
That small bit of attention changes everything. The same sip, gulped down over email, leaves no trace at all.
Stay for a moment with the aftertaste. Whatever's left on your tongue once the sip is gone.
Put the cup down, or keep it in your hands, and look up.
If there's a window, look outside. The sky, its exact color this morning. A rooftop, a tree, a building across the street, someone walking past.
If there's no window, look at the light in the room. Where it falls, what it touches.
No need to think about what you see. Just look, as if for the very first time.
[pause 3s]
Second sip. Notice whether it's different from the first. It often is. A little less hot, the flavor a little more present.
And maybe, somewhere in the background, part of you is getting impatient.
An urge to check the time. To run through today's to-do list. To finish up quickly and get on with things.
That's completely normal. In the morning, the mind loves to get ahead of itself.
Just notice that urge to hurry. You can even say to it, silently: I see you.
Then come back to the cup. To the warmth in your hands. That's all.
[pause 3s]
Take another sip or two, at your own pace. A sip, a glance outside. A sip, a breath.
Every time your mind races off toward the day ahead, the cup is right here to bring you back.
Notice how you feel now, compared to when you started. Maybe a little more settled. Maybe much the same. Both are fine.
What you just did, you can do again tomorrow. And the day after.
You have a drink every morning anyway. This moment is already part of your routine. All you need to add is your attention.
Even three mindful sips are a real practice. A way of starting the day by actually being in it, instead of already chasing after it.
Finish your cup however you like. And when you get up, take a little of this calm along with you.

sessions.title: Gentle wake-up
script: You've just opened your eyes, or nearly. Before you reach for your phone, stay lying down a little longer.
The notifications, the emails, the news: all of it can wait five minutes. This moment, between sleep and the day, belongs to you.
Waking up is a transition. If you jump straight into a screen, your body switches to alert mode before you're even out of bed. Here, we take the slower road.
If your eyes are open, you can close them again. Not to fall back asleep. Just to stay inside a little longer.
Start by feeling the bed. Its warmth, above all. The covers over you, their light weight on your shoulders, on your legs.
Notice where your body is warmest. Maybe your belly, the backs of your knees, your feet.
And where it's cooler. Your face, a hand poking out from the covers, the empty corner of the pillow.
Now notice the light behind your eyelids. Even with your eyes closed, you can sense it.
Is it fairly dark? Gray? Golden? Maybe it shifts slightly, as the sun moves or someone switches on a light next door.
Listen to the sounds as well. The quiet of the bedroom, a bird, a car, the city starting up, or the house creaking.
You don't have to do anything with them. Just let them come to you.
[pause 3s]
All through the night, your breathing took care of itself. Slow, steady, often quite shallow.
This morning, let's open it up gently. Breathe in a little more fully than usual, through your nose, letting your belly rise under the covers.
And breathe out, long and slow, through your mouth if you like.
Again. Breathe in, and this time let the air rise up into your chest, all the way to your collarbones.
Breathe out, and let your body sink a little deeper into the mattress.
[pause 3s]
A third time, at your own pace. No forcing. The in-breath opens, the out-breath settles.
Then let your breathing find its own rhythm again.
You might notice these fuller breaths warming you up a little, from the inside. They get you ready to move.
Now wake up your hands and feet. Start with your fingers. Barely move them, as if you were playing a quiet tune on the sheet.
Then slowly open and close your hands, joints still stiff with sleep.
Move on to your toes. Curl them up, then spread them wide. Once more.
You can make small circles with your wrists and ankles, one way, then the other.
It tells your body: we're waking up, but there's no hurry.
And now, stretch. Like a cat getting up from a nap. No set order, no right way.
You can reach your arms overhead and push your heels away, making yourself long.
You can roll onto your side, round your back, or stretch one leg and then the other.
Hold each stretch for two or three seconds, then let it go all at once, like a sigh.
Listen for what your body wants this morning. Maybe your back. Maybe your shoulders. Maybe a big yawn: let it come, it's part of the stretch.
[pause 3s]
Let everything go. Settle onto your back, or your side, whichever you prefer.
Notice the difference. Warmth moving through you, a little more space in your joints, a slightly clearer head.

If thoughts about the day start arriving, the list, the time, what's ahead, that's normal. You don't have to push them away. Just tell them: later. And come back to the warmth of the bed, to the breath coming and going.
Before you get up, choose a phrase for your day. Something short and simple that you could say to yourself again later.
For example: "I have time to do one thing at a time." Or: "I'm starting gently." Or a phrase that comes from you.
Say it once, silently, on an out-breath.
[pause 3s]
Now open your eyes, if they aren't open already. Let the light in, little by little.
Roll onto your side. Press into the mattress with your hands, and slowly come up to sitting on the edge of the bed.
Put your feet on the floor. Feel the coolness of the wood, the tiles or the rug under the soles of your feet.
Stay there for a breath or two before you stand.
Feel your weight settle into your feet. Your back lengthens, your head rests easily above your shoulders. You can stand up whenever you're ready.
Your day has begun gently. Keep that pace for as long as you can.

sessions.title: Waking up anxious
script: You woke up with that knot in your stomach. Your heart a little fast, your mind already racing, before you've even put a foot on the floor.
If that's how it is this morning, you're in the right place. And it's one of the most common ways to wake up.
Notice one thing, to begin with. Nothing has happened yet. The day hasn't started. For now, there's just you, here, and this feeling.
You can stay lying down or sit up, whatever you prefer. Keep your eyes open, resting on something calm: the ceiling, a corner of the wall, the light at the window.

A quick word about what's going on. In the morning, your body is starting up. To pull you out of sleep, it naturally turns up its level of activation. Your heart speeds up a little, your mind becomes alert.
That's a normal process, and it's there to help you get going.

But when you're going through a busy or difficult stretch, that start-up can feel a lot like worry. Your body is on alert, and your mind goes looking for a reason: the ten o'clock meeting, the email you haven't answered, yesterday's conversation.
So what you're feeling isn't necessarily a message about your day. Partly, it's just your body waking up a bit too loudly.
Just knowing that can ease things a little. You don't have to work out what's wrong right away. You can take care of your body first.
Let's help it turn the volume down. Place one hand on your belly, just below your navel. The other can rest on your chest, or on the bed.
Feel the warmth of your hand. Its weight. It's there, it's not going anywhere.
Breathe in normally through your nose. No need to take in a lot of air.
Then breathe out slowly through your mouth, as if you were cooling a spoonful of hot soup. Longer than the in-breath.
[pause 3s]
Again. Breathe in simply… and let the out-breath stretch out, easy, all the way to the end.
Under your hand, your belly sinks back down.
Notice the small release that often comes at the end of the out-breath, in your shoulders or your jaw.
Why the out-breath? Lengthening it sends your body a signal of safety. A bit like gently easing your foot off the accelerator.
Keep going at your own pace. The in-breath stays natural; it's the out-breath that gets longer. You can count in your head if it helps: in for three, out for five or six.
If it feels difficult, or you feel dizzy, just go back to your normal breathing. There's nothing to get right.
[pause 3s]
Now look at the anxiety a little more closely, without diving into it. The way you'd look out the window to check the weather.
You can give it a simple name. "Worry." "Tension." "Dread about the day." Whatever word fits.
Naming it silently is already taking a tiny step back from it.
Then find where it lives in your body. Your stomach? Your throat? Your chest? Your jaw?
Notice its shape. Is it a weight, a knot, a restlessness, a heat?
You don't have to make it go away. It can stay right there, while your hand keeps breathing along with you.
[pause 3s]
Now, a useful distinction. On one side, what's actually going to happen today. On the other, what your mind is busy imagining.
Think about what's on your mind. Then ask yourself: what do I know for certain, right now, concretely?
Maybe: "I have a meeting at two o'clock." That's a fact.
And then there's the story wrapped around it: "It's going to go badly. I won't cope. Everyone will see." Those are scenarios. Guesses your mind produces, especially when your body is on alert.
You don't have to argue with these thoughts. Just recognize them: ah, that one's a scenario.
And come back to the fact, which is usually smaller, simpler, and more doable.
[pause 3s]
There's another truth here too: you've already made it through days you were dreading. And here you are.
This morning, you don't need to have all the answers before you get up either. You just need the next step.
So we're not going to plan the whole day. We're going to choose just one thing. The very first, and the smallest possible.
Drink a glass of water. Open the window and feel the fresh air on your face. Put on your slippers. Switch on the kitchen light.
Pick one. Whichever feels easiest, right here, right now.
Picture yourself doing it. The cool glass in your hand, or the air drifting into the room.
This tiny step matters more than it seems. It brings your body back into concrete action, where worry has less of a grip.
[pause 3s]
Before you get up, take two more breaths with that long out-breath. Hand on your belly.
Notice whether anything has shifted, even slightly. Sometimes the knot loosens a little. Sometimes it stays, and that's okay too. You can get up and take it with you.
If anxious mornings like this come back very often or weigh on your daily life, it's worth talking to a health professional.
For this morning, there's only one thing to do: that first small step. Then the next one. One thing at a time.
Okay. Sit up slowly, put your feet on the floor, and go do your first small thing.

sessions.title: Morning gratitude
script: Hello, and good morning. Settle in just as you are, sitting on your bed, on a chair, or still lying down if you'd rather.
Let your hands rest wherever they're comfortable. Close your eyes, or simply let your gaze drift down toward the floor.
Take one breath that's a little fuller than the others. And as you breathe out, let your shoulders drop a notch.
Then let your breathing do whatever it wants. Calm, or a bit quick, it doesn't matter. Just follow it for a few moments.
The air coming in, slightly cool in your nostrils. The air going out, a little warmer.
If thoughts are already drifting in, the day, the time, your to-do list, let them pass through. You'll get back to them later. For now, just the breath.
[pause 3s]
Before we begin, a word about why.

Your attention has a natural habit: it spots what's wrong first. The problem to fix, the delay, the criticism. That's useful for keeping you safe, but first thing in the morning, it can tint the whole day gray.
Gratitude is an attention practice. Not to deny what's hard. Just to notice, as well, what's holding you up, the things that so often go unnoticed.
This morning, we're going to look for three thank-yous. Not vague ones. Precise, detailed thank-yous that you can really feel.
The first is very simple. Something material, everyday, that you used this morning or during the night.
Your bed, for example. The mattress that held you up for hours, the duvet that kept you warm.
Or the hot water from the tap. The fact that all it takes is turning a handle for it to flow, at just the right temperature.
Choose your thing. And now make it precise. Its texture, its smell, the sound it makes. The exact moment you enjoyed it.
Imagine this morning without it for a second. A hard bed, a cold shower. Suddenly, this small, ordinary thing takes on a different place.
Think of how many people worked so that this thing could be here. The people who made it, shipped it, installed it.
And say thank you to it, silently. A simple thank-you, like the one you'd give someone holding a door for you.
[pause 3s]
The second thank-you goes to a person. Someone who matters to you, or someone who simply helped you recently. A loved one, a colleague, the person at the bakery who smiled at you.
Let their face appear. Look at their eyes, their expression, the way they hold themselves.
If several faces come to mind, choose just one for today. The others will have their turn another morning.
Remember a specific moment with them. Something they said, a gesture, a message that arrived at just the right time.
What does this person bring you? Laughter, calm, confidence, a helping hand?
Thank them, silently, as if they were standing in front of you. You can even imagine their reaction as they hear it.
You don't need to tell them for this thank-you to count. Simply thinking it already shifts how you see them, and your day, a little.
[pause 3s]
The third thank-you is for you. That may feel strange, and it's often the hardest one. Take your time.
It could be a quality. Your patience, your sense of humor, your curiosity, the way you look after others.
Or your body. Your legs that carry you all day long. Your hands that know how to do a thousand things. Your heart that has been beating, without you having to think about it, since day one.
Choose just one thing. And thank it, the way you'd thank a loyal friend.
Think of a recent moment when it helped you. Yesterday, maybe. A specific situation where this quality, or this body, was there for you.
If a little voice protests or plays it down, that's okay. Notice it, and come back to your thank-you.
[pause 3s]
Now let these three thank-yous come together. The simple thing. The person. What's in you.
Place a hand on the center of your chest, if you like.
Notice what's happening there. Maybe a gentle warmth. A sense of openness, of softness. Maybe a smile finding its way onto your face.
Or maybe nothing special, and that's just as good. Gratitude doesn't need to be dramatic to count.
Research suggests that practicing gratitude regularly may help people feel a little more at ease. But this morning, there's no result to chase: just this moment.
Breathe with whatever is here. Breathe in, and let your chest open a little. Breathe out, and let that feeling spread, toward your shoulders, toward your belly.
[pause 3s]
Stay here for a few more breaths. Nothing to add, nothing to look for.
The breath carries on, simple. Any warmth in your chest can just stay there, without you having to hold on to it.
Before you get up, choose one of these three thank-yous to carry with you. The one that touches you most this morning.
You can come back to it at some point today. On the train, at your desk, standing in line. It takes three seconds.
And if you feel like it, you could even say it out loud. Send a quick message to the person you thought of, for instance.
Gently, come back to the room. Move your fingers, stretch your back a little.
Open your eyes, and look around you. Maybe a fourth thank-you is already waiting for you somewhere.

sessions.title: Preview your day
script: This morning, before the day sweeps you along, let's take a quick tour of it. The way you'd look at a route on a map before setting off.
The idea isn't to plan everything. It's to spot the tricky stretch, and to arrive there with a plan.
It's not about worrying ahead of time. Quite the opposite: a moment you've already looked at squarely is often less scary than one you avoid imagining.
Sit down, back supported, feet flat. You can close your eyes, or rest your gaze softly on a point in front of you.
Take three easy breaths. In through the nose… and out a little more slowly.
[pause 3s]
Once more. Feel the air coming in, and your body settling into the chair as you breathe out.
One last one. Then let your breathing carry on by itself.
Feel what's supporting you. Feet on the floor, thighs on the seat, back against the chair. This is your base. You can come back to it at any moment.
If your mind is already busy this morning, that's normal. It has a lot on its plate. This exercise will give it some structure: we look, we choose, we prepare.
Now run through your day in your head. Quickly, like a film on fast-forward. No need for detail.
Start with the rest of your morning. Shower, breakfast, getting dressed. Maybe a commute: the street, the bus, the train, the car.
Then arriving. At work, at school, or at your desk if you work from home. The first tasks, the first conversations.
Move forward to lunchtime. Where will you eat? Who with?
Then the afternoon. Meetings, calls, things that are due.
And the end of the day. Heading home, the evening, the moment you finally put your bag down.
Notice how many different moments fit into a single day. It's rarely just one big block.
If some hours are hazy, that's fine. Just stick to the main stages. And notice, as you pass over each one, how you feel: neutral, curious, tense, impatient.
[pause 3s]
As you skimmed through, one moment may have caught your attention. The one where you felt a slight tightening, a flinch, an "oh no."
It might be a meeting, a call you're dreading, a delicate conversation, a big task, or simply the six o'clock rush.
Pick just one. Ideally something moderately difficult, not the worst thing in your week.
Place it. What time is it? Where are you? Who's there?
Notice how your body reacts just from thinking about it. Shoulders creeping up, stomach tightening, jaw clenching. That's information, nothing more.
Before going further, let one long out-breath soften whatever tensed up. Shoulders dropping. Jaw loosening.
[pause 3s]
Now we're going to rehearse that moment. Like an athlete picturing the race before the start.
See yourself arriving in that situation. But this time, pay attention to your posture. Your back is upright, your feet steady on the ground. Your shoulders are low. Your hands relaxed.
Your breathing is slow. Before walking in, or just as it begins, you take one long, quiet out-breath. Nobody notices.
Let the scene unfold. What people say to you, how you reply. You take a moment before speaking. Your voice is steady.
Notice the details. The light in the room, the chair you're sitting in, the mug in front of you. The more precise the scene, the more familiar it will feel when the moment comes.
Maybe there's a tense moment. A comment, a tricky question, something unexpected. See yourself taking it in, pausing briefly, and answering at your own pace.
You don't have to be flawless in this scene. Just present and calm, in your own way.
If your mind heads for the worst, gently steer the scene back to a simple, realistic version. Not perfect, not a disaster.
[pause 3s]
Now turn that into a simple plan. A plan in two parts: if… then…
The first part is the signal. The moment you notice the pressure rising. For example: "If I feel my throat tighten…" Or: "If someone talks over me…" Or: "If I see that pile of files…"

The second part is your response. Something tiny and concrete. "Then I plant my feet and breathe out slowly." "Then I take a sip of water before answering." "Then I start with one task, the smallest one."
Choose a response you can actually do on the spot, discreetly, even with other people around. A breath, a gesture, a phrase you say to yourself.
Now write your own plan. Pick your words. Keep it short.
Say it once, silently, slowly. If… then…
[pause 3s]
A small prepared phrase like this can really help. When the moment comes, you don't have to search for a solution in the middle of the pressure: it's already there, ready to use.
Run through the scene one last time, with your plan. The signal arrives… and you use your response. Simple.
The more you rehearse it like this, the more natural it becomes. Like a route you take every day, one your feet know by heart.
Before we finish, take one more quick tour. But this time, look for something pleasant.

There's almost always something, even on a packed day. A coffee with a colleague. Lunch. A call with someone you love. The ride home with a good podcast. That first step into your living room in the evening.
Pick it. And picture it already. The taste, the laughter, the light, the relief.
Decide to really savor it when it comes. Not thinking about what's next. Just living it.
[pause 3s]
Now come back to what's supporting you. Feet, thighs, back. The breath coming and going.
You've already taken a full tour of your day. You know where the tricky stretch is, and you have your plan. You also know where the good moment is waiting.
And if the day turns out differently than expected, your plan still works. The signal might show up somewhere else, at another time: the response stays the same.
Whatever else happens, you'll adapt, the way you always do.
Take one last breath, long and easy. Feel your body in the chair, ready to get up.
Gently move your hands, your shoulders. Open your eyes.
And keep your little phrase in your pocket. If… then… It's there when you need it.

sessions.title: Set your intention
script: Good morning. Today, we're going to choose a word. Just one. The one that will help you stay yourself, whatever the day has in store.
Sit upright, tall without being stiff. You might picture your spine as a stack of coins, balanced one on top of the other.
Rest your hands on your thighs, palms down, or open toward the sky, whichever you prefer.
Let your eyes close, or lower your gaze to the floor, about an arm's length in front of you.
Think of this as a small threshold between the night and the day. Before the messages, before the obligations, a moment to choose your direction.
Start by listening to your breath, without changing it. Just notice where you feel it most clearly this morning.
Maybe at the rim of your nostrils, with the cool air coming in. Maybe in your chest as it rises. Maybe in your belly.
Choose that spot and stay with it for a few breaths.
Feel the small resting moment that arrives on its own at the end of the out-breath. No need to stretch it. Just notice it.
If thoughts drift by, the shopping list, an email, yesterday's conversation, let them pass. Come back to the place where you feel your breath. Coming back is the practice.
Let your body settle as well. Feet on the floor, weight on the seat, hands heavy on your thighs. Nothing else to do, for now, but sit here and breathe.
Now ask yourself a question. Not "what do I have to do today?" You already know that; your to-do list has it covered.
The question is more like this: how do I want to be, today?
In the way I speak to people. The way I work. The way I respond when something doesn't go to plan.
You can also put it another way. Tonight, as you get into bed, what would you like to be able to say about how you lived this day?
Let the question float. Don't hunt for the answer with your head. Wait for it to come.
This isn't one more goal to hit. It's more like a compass: a gentle direction you can come back to when the day pulls you off course.
[pause 3s]
Maybe a word has already appeared. If so, welcome it, even if it surprises you.
If not, here are a few suggestions. Listen, and notice which one resonates.
Patience.
Presence.
Courage.
Gentleness.
Clarity.
Lightness.
Trust.
There's no right or wrong word. What matters is the one that fits what you need today, not the one you think you ought to pick.
And if none of these speak to you, another word may come. "Openness." "Simplicity." "Listening." Or even an image.
You may find yourself torn between two words. Choose the one that feels a little kinder when you say it, the one that eases you rather than the one that piles on pressure.
[pause 3s]
Do you have your word? Say it to yourself once, slowly.

Behind every word, there's often a value. Something that matters to you. If you chose "patience," maybe it's because you care about the quality of your relationships. If it's "courage," maybe it's because you want to move forward on something important.
Ask yourself: why this word, this morning? What does it protect, or what does it make possible?
Now look for this word in your body. What does patience, or trust, or lightness, feel like physically?
Maybe your shoulders drop a little. Your chest opens. Your jaw unclenches. Your breathing becomes slower, or fuller.
If nothing clear shows up, simply imagine you're already living this word. How would you be sitting? How would you be breathing?
Let your body take the shape of your word. Adjust your posture slightly, if you feel like it.
Notice where the sensation is clearest. Remember that spot: that's where your word lives.
[pause 3s]
Now think of one specific moment in your day when this word could be useful. Just one.
Maybe a meeting that's likely to drag on, if your word is "patience." A conversation you've been putting off, if it's "courage." Dinner with your kids or the people you love, if it's "presence."
See that moment. The place, the time, the people around you.
Then imagine your word walking into the scene with you. It doesn't change anyone else. It changes something small in you: a second's pause before you reply, a softer look, a step forward.
If something difficult comes up in the scene, see yourself coming back to your word, the way you'd reach for the handrail on a staircase. One breath is enough.
Watch how the moment unfolds, with your word by your side. Notice how you feel at the end.
Notice that you didn't need to become someone else. Your word simply helped you stay a little more yourself.
[pause 3s]
Come back to your breath. Now we'll anchor your word over three out-breaths.
Breathe in easily… and as you breathe out, say your word silently.
[pause 3s]
Breathe in… and on the out-breath, your word again. Let it sink down with the air.
[pause 3s]
One last time. Breathe in… and your word, all the way through the out-breath.
[pause 3s]
Stay for a moment with what's here. The word, the feeling in your body, the quiet of the morning.
You don't have to embody this word all day long. You'll forget it, that's a given. What matters is coming back to it now and then.
And this word isn't there to judge you. If tonight you feel you lacked patience or courage, that's not a failure. Tomorrow, you can choose the same word, or another one.

To help you remember, give yourself a discreet reminder. Write the word on a sticky note and put it on your screen or your mirror. Make it your phone wallpaper. Or link it to something you do often, like opening a door or drinking water.
Each time you come across that reminder: one breath, and your word.
These small reminders matter. Without them, the morning's word gets lost in the noise of the day. With them, it comes back.
Gently, come back to the room. Move your fingers and toes. Sit up a little taller, and stretch your neck to one side, then the other.
Whenever you're ready, open your eyes. Your word is chosen. It's just waiting for you.

sessions.title: Mindful morning stretch
script: Welcome to these eight minutes for loosening up your body. If you feel stiff this morning, or if sitting still to meditate feels like a struggle, this session is for you.
Here, we meditate by moving. Movement becomes the anchor, and the breath sets the pace.
One rule, and only one, before we start: never into pain. Always stay within what's comfortable. If a movement doesn't suit you, make it smaller, or just do it in your imagination.
And if standing isn't possible for you, you can follow the whole session on a chair, sitting slightly forward, away from the backrest.
Stand with your feet hip-width apart. Toes pointing forward. Knees soft, not locked.
Let your arms hang by your sides. Feel the weight of your hands at the ends of your arms.
Bring your attention to your feet. Heels, soles, toes. Where is most of your weight resting? Maybe more on one foot than the other, more on your heels than the balls of your feet.
Sway very slightly, forward and back, then side to side, and find the center. The place where you can stand without effort.
This gentle swaying already wakes up your ankles and leg muscles. They're the ones carrying you through this session.
Take a breath. Just notice what it's like this morning. Short, long, high in the chest, low in the belly.
From here on, we'll let the breath guide every movement. The in-breath opens and lifts. The out-breath releases and lowers.
If you slept in a slightly awkward position, you may notice a particular stiffness, in your neck or lower back. Keep it in mind, and take extra care of that area.
First movement. As you breathe in, slowly raise your arms out to the sides, then up over your head.
Your palms can meet, or stay shoulder-width apart.
As you breathe out, let your arms come back down the same way, like a big wave.
[pause 3s]
Again. Breathe in, arms rising. Feel the space opening between your ribs, the air filling the top of your chest.
Breathe out, arms lowering. Shoulders stay well away from your ears.
Do two or three more of these waves at your own pace. Match the speed of your arms to the length of your breath. If the in-breath is short, the movement is short.
No need to fill your lungs to the max. We're looking for a smooth movement, not a feat.
[pause 3s]
Now, side bends. Breathe in, and raise your right arm over your head. Your left hand slides down the outside of your left thigh.
As you breathe out, lean gently to the left. Like a tree bending in the wind.
Feel the stretch all along your right side, from your hip to your fingertips.
Keep both feet firmly grounded. Don't try to go far: a small arc is plenty.
Breathe here. With each in-breath, imagine the air flowing into the ribs on the stretched side.
[pause 3s]
Breathe in, and come back to center. Breathe out, arm lowering.
Now the other side. Breathe in, left arm rising. Breathe out, leaning to the right.
Notice whether this side feels different. Looser, or stiffer. The body is never perfectly symmetrical, and that's absolutely fine.
[pause 3s]
Breathe in, back to center. Breathe out, arm lowering.
Now, a forward roll-down. Bend your knees a little more. This matters, to protect your lower back.
As you breathe out, let your chin drop toward your chest. Then your shoulders round, and your back rolls down, one vertebra at a time.
Your arms hang heavy toward the floor. No need to touch your toes. Stop wherever feels comfortable, even halfway.
Let your head hang, neck relaxed. You can nod a small yes, then shake a small no, to release the back of your neck.
Breathe into your back. Feel it lengthen and widen with every in-breath.
If you like, bend one knee and then the other, alternating, to gently stretch the backs of your legs. No bouncing.
[pause 3s]
To come up, press firmly into your feet. Over several breaths, roll your back up, one vertebra at a time. Your head comes up last.
Take your time. If you feel a little dizzy as you come up, stay still for a moment, knees soft, and breathe normally.
Now, some gentle twists. Let your arms hang loose, relaxed like scarves.
Turn your upper body gently to the right, then to the left. Your arms follow, lightly tapping against your body as they swing.
Your feet stay put. Your hips can follow a little. Your gaze goes along with the movement.
Let the rhythm find itself. Like a child playing at swinging their arms.
Your breath follows freely. You don't need to count it.
Notice the feeling in your lower back, around your waist. That's often where the night has left some stiffness, and the movement eases it, little by little.
[pause 3s]
Slow down gradually. Smaller and smaller twists, until you come to rest at the center.
Take a moment to feel your lower back, still now. It often feels warmer and looser than at the start.
Now, a chest opener. Bring your hands behind your back. Interlace your fingers if you can. If not, hold one wrist, or grip both ends of a towel.
As you breathe in, gently draw your hands down and away from your back. Your shoulder blades move toward each other. Your chest opens forward, as if you were turning it toward the sun.
Keep your neck long, chin level with the floor.
Breathe here for a few breaths. Feel the fronts of your shoulders stretching, right where all those hours hunched over a screen tend to settle.
[pause 3s]
As you breathe out, release your hands. Let your arms come back to your sides.
Roll your shoulders once or twice, to finish.
Now, stay still. Remain standing, eyes closed or gaze resting on the floor.
Feel what's happening in your body after moving. Tingling in your hands. Warmth in your back. Your heartbeat, a little more noticeable.
Maybe there's more space in your chest, more length along your sides.
Feel your feet again. Is your weight spread differently than it was at the start?
Notice your breath too. It may have found a fuller rhythm, without you even trying.
This body that felt stiff a few minutes ago is now a little more alive. You didn't force anything. You simply listened to it.
Your body has its own wisdom. It knows what does it good, when you give it time to tell you.
[pause 3s]
Take one last full breath, raising your arms one more time, if you feel like it.
And as you breathe out, let them float back down, slowly.
Feel your feet on the ground one last time, before picking up the thread of your morning.

Carry this looser body with you into your day. And when the stiffness creeps back, at your computer or on your commute, remember: a single side bend, a single roll-down, a single breath, and you can find a little of this ease again.
Even two minutes of stretching tomorrow morning can change the way you start your day.
Have a good day. Take it gently.

sessions.title: Slow weekend morning
script: It's the weekend. Or a day off, a morning with no alarm and no appointments.
Today, there's no rush. Nothing to do, nowhere to be. For these ten minutes, you have permission to accomplish absolutely nothing.
You might still be in bed, in an armchair, by a window, out on a balcony. Choose wherever your body wants to be. And settle in as if for a long while.
If someone is still asleep beside you, or the house is waking up around you, that's fine. You can listen quietly: this moment is still yours.
Start by noticing where you are. The surface holding you up. The temperature of the air. What you're wearing, pajamas, a blanket, an old sweater.
There's no ideal posture this morning. If you want to pull your knees up, lean back against a cushion, let your head tilt to one side, go ahead.
Let your body find its most comfortable position, the one you'd choose if nobody were watching.
Now, a curious observation. Even though nothing is urgent, part of you may still be running.
Listen from the inside. Have your thoughts already started planning? Groceries, laundry, messages to send, all the things you should do this weekend to "make the most of it"?
Is your body a little ahead of itself? A slight tightness in your chest, a clenched jaw, an itch to get up and do something?

That's very common. After a busy week, the body holds on to its momentum, like a train that keeps rolling after the engine's been switched off. Alert mode doesn't shut down all at once, just because it's Saturday.
You don't have to chase it away. Just notice it. Oh, look. I'm still running.

You might even notice, with a bit of humor, all the little voices saying you should get up, tidy up, get things done. They're used to running the week. This morning, they can sit next to you, without taking the wheel.
There's nothing wrong with you for still feeling the pull. It's just the rhythm of the week, taking a little while to wind down.
So, let's slow down. Very gradually.
First, the breath. No technique here. Just let each out-breath last a tiny bit longer. Like a lazy sigh.
Breathe in… and let the air drift out without hurrying, all the way to the end.
[pause 3s]
Again. The in-breath comes on its own. The out-breath takes its time.
And at the end of the out-breath, there's sometimes a small moment of stillness, before the next in-breath arrives. You don't need to make it happen. Just notice it, if it's there.
Place a hand on your belly if you like, and feel it rise and fall, slowly. Like a wave stretching up the sand, then drawing back without any hurry.
[pause 3s]
Now, your movements. If you move, move at half your usual speed.
If you're holding a mug, bring it to your lips as if in slow motion. If you change position, do it as if you were underwater.
Try it with your hand now. Lift it very slowly, just a few inches, and set it back down. Notice everything you feel during that simple movement. The lightness, the weight, the air on your skin.
At weekends, we often fill our free time just as quickly as everything else. Slowing your movements is a way of telling your body: today, we have time. Really.
This slowness might feel strange at first. Maybe even a bit uncomfortable. That's a sign you're stepping out of autopilot.
If the urge to hurry comes back, notice it, and slow down just a little more. Not out of discipline. Out of curiosity.
And now, let yourself savor what's here. The sensations of the morning, one at a time.
The light, first. If your eyes are open, look at it. How does it come into the room? Through the window, between the curtains, as a beam or a soft veil?
Notice its color. In the morning, it's often softer, more golden, or a pale, peaceful gray. Watch how it rests on things, the wall, the floor. The shadows it draws.
Maybe a speck of dust is dancing in a sunbeam. Maybe a reflection is trembling on the ceiling. Tiny shows that play out every morning, often with no one watching.
If your eyes are closed, feel the light through your eyelids. A tint, a brightness.
[pause 3s]
Then the warmth. Where is your body nice and warm? Under the blanket, around a mug, where the sun touches your skin?
Let yourself enjoy that warmth, simply. Like a cat settling into a patch of sunlight. It has nothing else to do. Neither do you.
Notice the contrast, too. One part warm, another cooler. Your nose a little chilly, your feet tucked under the covers. Those small differences make the warmth even more pleasant.
And the sounds. Listen to the morning. At weekends, it often sounds different.
Maybe fewer cars. Birds more noticeable. Neighbors laughing, a child playing, a market setting up, church bells in the distance. The coffee machine gurgling, the cat jumping off the sofa.
You don't need to name them. Let them come to you, and go again. The near ones, the far ones, and the silence in between.
Choose one sound, and follow it until it fades. Listen to the very end, the moment it melts into everything else.
Sounds make a lovely anchor on a slow morning. They arrive without any effort, and they're always new.
[pause 3s]
And maybe a smell. Coffee, toast, fresh air drifting in through a half-open window. Or just the familiar smell of home.
Breathe in gently, without searching. Let the smell come to you, rather than going looking for it.
Now I'll guide a little less. There's nothing in particular to notice anymore.
Let your attention open up, like a window flung wide. Everything can come in. Sounds, sensations, light, passing thoughts.
Nothing to hold on to, nothing to push away. Just be here, in the middle of it all.
You could imagine sitting on a riverbank. Everything that passes, sounds, thoughts, sensations, drifts by on the water. You watch, and let it flow.
If you catch yourself planning, smile at the habit, and come back to the morning.
You can let your gaze rest somewhere, without fixing on anything. Or close your eyes. Your body is heavy, your breath finds its own way.
[pause 5s]
One breath… and you stay right here.
[pause 4s]
Notice that this moment doesn't need anything more. No goal, no progress to make. Just the morning, and you in it.
All is well. There's nowhere else you need to be.
If a thought carries you off, it's nothing. You notice, you come back. And the morning is still here, waiting for you.
Maybe the light has already shifted a little since we began. Maybe a new sound has appeared. The morning moves slowly around you, and all you have to do is let it.
[pause 5s]
Gently, bring a little attention back to yourself. And ask yourself a question, without rushing for an answer.
What would really do me good today?
Not what would be productive. Not what you "should" do. What would actually do you good.
Maybe a long walk. A bath. A book. Seeing a friend. Cooking without watching the clock. Or nothing at all, which is a perfectly good answer.
You can also ask: what does my body need? To move, to rest, to eat something delicious, to be outside? And what does my heart need? Quiet, laughter, company?
Listen to what comes. Sometimes it's a specific wish, sometimes just a feeling: more air, more calm, more connection.
If nothing comes, that's fine. The question can keep working quietly in the background while you have breakfast or take a shower.
[pause 3s]
Hold that wish lightly. It's not another task to tick off. It's an invitation.
It doesn't matter if the day doesn't go exactly the way you picture it. The point isn't to get your weekend right. It's to stay a little closer to yourself.
And if, later on, you feel the pace picking up again for no reason, you can come back to what you did this morning. A lazy out-breath. A slow-motion gesture. One sound you really listen to.
Before you move, stay here a moment longer. Notice what it feels like to have taken this time. Even if nothing special happened.
Maybe that's exactly the point. That nothing happened.
You've just given your body something rare: time without a goal. It often holds on to that, a kind of ease that lingers for a while.
When you feel like it, and not before, start to move. Slowly. Stretch, if you're in the mood.
Arms overhead, a long yawn, your whole body lengthening.
And try to give yourself mornings like this more often. Even ten minutes, on a Tuesday, before the house wakes up.
For now, step into your day at the pace of this morning. There's no race to win today.

sessions.title: Walking meditation
script: This meditation is done while walking. Outdoors, on your way to work, in a park, or simply at home, pacing back and forth across your living room or along a hallway.

First, a safety note. Keep your eyes open the whole time. If you're outside, stay aware of what's around you: sidewalks, bikes, cars. At crossings, look, and cross as you normally would, with your full attention on the road. And of course, never while driving.
Your inner chatter can quiet down. The world around you stays switched on.
If you're outside, listen with one earbud, or at low volume, so you can still hear the street.
To begin, stand still for a moment. Feet hip-width apart, arms by your sides.
Notice your posture too. Knees soft, pelvis settled, shoulders dropping naturally. Your head light, as if balanced on top of your spine.
Feel the weight of your body sinking down into your feet. How is it spread? More on your heels? More toward the front? More on one foot than the other?
Sway gently, forward and back, side to side. Then find the center, the point where your weight is spread roughly evenly over both feet.
Feel the ground beneath you. Hard, soft, flat, uneven. The contact of your sole, your sock, or bare skin.
Take a moment to really feel it. This contact with the ground will be your anchor throughout.
[pause 3s]
Take a breath or two here. Your gaze resting a few yards ahead, not fixed on anything.
This short pause helps your mind change gears. You shift from "I need to get there" to "I'm walking right now."

Now, let's start walking. Very slowly at first. Much more slowly than usual. If you're on the street and this pace feels awkward, just walk a little slower than normal, and keep your attention in your feet.
Shift your weight onto your left leg. Feel your right leg becoming light.
Your right heel lifts. Then the sole. Then your toes leave the ground.
Your foot moves forward through the air, a few inches.
And comes down. Heel first. Then the sole rolls down. Then the toes.
Your weight glides forward, onto that right foot. And your left leg, in turn, becomes light.

Breaking it down like this may feel mechanical at first, a bit like learning to walk all over again. That's normal. You're discovering a movement you've made all your life, without ever really watching it.
[pause 3s]
Keep going like this, step by step. Heel, sole, toes. Lift, move, place.
You can say it silently, if it helps. "Lift… move… place."
Notice all the tiny adjustments your body makes to keep its balance. Ankles, calves, hips. An incredible feat of coordination you perform thousands of times a day without a thought.
Notice, too, the moment when both feet are on the ground at once, just before your weight tips forward. A tiny instant of double support, and then the movement carries on.
[pause 3s]
If you're at home and you reach the end of the room, stop for a moment. Feel your feet, still. Then turn around slowly, staying present through the whole turn. And set off again.
The turn is part of the walk too. Your weight shifting, your feet pivoting, your eyes discovering the other side of the room.
Now, link your breath to your steps. Not rigidly. Just noticing the connection between them.
For example, you might breathe in over two steps, and out over two steps. Or in over three, out over four. Find whatever feels natural.
Breathe in… one step, two steps. Breathe out… one step, two steps.
If your breath needs more or less, let it decide. Your steps adapt to your breath, not the other way around.
Notice whether your breathing slows a little as your steps become steady. Or whether it stays the same. Either is fine.
[pause 3s]
Keep walking with this rhythm. Breath and feet moving together, like two musicians playing the same tune.
If counting steps feels too much like school, drop the numbers. Just feel the in-breath carrying a few steps, and the out-breath carrying a few more.
[pause 3s]
You may have noticed that your mind has already wandered off. Toward your day, a memory, a conversation, a project.
That's perfectly normal. It's what minds do. There's nothing to fix.
The moment you realize it, that's already a moment of presence. Simply come back to your feet. To the next heel touching the ground.
You can even note, in one word, where your mind went. "Work." "Memory." "Worry." Then pick up your stride again, no commentary needed.
[pause 3s]
Now widen your attention a little. Your feet stay as a reference point, in the background. But you open up your other senses too.
Sounds first. What's close by, your own footsteps, the rustle of your clothes. Then further away: voices, a door, wind in the trees, traffic, a bird, a fridge humming.
Let them come, without holding on to them.
Notice how they change as you move. Some come closer, others fade and disappear behind you.
The air on your skin. On your face, on your hands. Cool, mild, damp, dry. Maybe a bit of a breeze. Maybe sunshine on one cheek.
And smells, if you notice any. Coffee from a café, damp earth, cut grass, warm bread from a bakery, or the familiar smell of your hallway.
No need to stop to take them in. They come to you, step by step.

And colors. Look around as if you were discovering this place for the first time. The green of the leaves, the gray of the pavement, the red of a mailbox, the blue or white of the sky. At home, the color of a book, a cushion, a plant.
Let one color draw you in. Really look at it for a few seconds, while you keep walking.
If you're outside, notice the other people passing by. Each with their own day, their own thoughts, their own pace. You're part of this great morning movement, simply by walking.
[pause 3s]
All of this is part of your walk. You walk, and the world flows in through your senses.
If at any point it feels like too much at once, come back to your feet. Heel, sole, toes. That's your anchor, always available.
[pause 3s]

Thoughts will almost certainly come back, again and again. Each time, it's the same: you notice, and you come back to your feet. No frustration, no judgment. The way you'd gently bring back a puppy that's wandered off.
This coming back is the real heart of the practice. It's not a failure. It's the exercise itself.
Maybe your mind is calmer now, or maybe it's still very busy. Either way, your walk is exactly what it needs to be.
Now you can let your pace pick up. Gradually return to your natural walking speed. Your everyday pace.
This is where the real challenge begins. At this speed, the mind is used to slipping into autopilot.
Let's see if you can keep a little presence. Not as much as when you were walking slowly. Just a thread.
Keep feeling your foot meet the ground with each step, even at this faster pace. The natural swing of your arms. Your breath adjusting to the new rhythm.
You could choose a cue to bring you back to the present. For example, every time you pass a tree, a red light or a doorway. That cue becomes your bell: one mindful step, then you carry on.
[pause 3s]
Notice how you're holding yourself. Is your head pushed forward, as if it wanted to arrive before you? Let it come back over your shoulders. Your gaze opens out toward the horizon.
Let your arms swing freely too, rather than burying them in your pockets or clenching them around your bag.
An open posture often changes how you meet what comes next. Your body straightens, and your mind follows.
A few more steps, at your own pace. Feet, breath, sounds, light. Everything is here, all at once.
If you reach a street to cross, set the meditation aside while you cross. Look, wait, cross. Then pick up the thread again.
[pause 3s]
This session is coming to an end, but your walk can carry on.
If you're outside, you can keep this attention all the way to where you're going. The station, the office, the bakery. At least now and then, come back to a step, a sound, a color.
If you're at home, come to a gentle stop. Stand for a few seconds. Feel your weight settle back into both feet, still.
Notice your body after this walk. What feels calmer, more awake, more present.
This morning, you walked without rushing toward what's next. You lived in the journey, instead of just getting through it.
From today, every journey can become a small meditation. Even two minutes, between your front door and the end of the street.
Or along an office corridor, between two meetings.
All you need is to remember your feet. They're always there, with every step, to bring you back here.
